body_markdown:
The[latest question](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/our-two-cents/) I posed to my coworkers was far from straightforward, but I knew we had thoughts worthy of sharing. That’s because there’s a lot to see in a decade of car culture, as automobiles encompass just about anything else you’d experience in a specific time period in many locations around the world. But the question is vague on purpose, because I wanted to ensure that the answers were as varied and enlightening as possible.


The two criteria I insisted upon were also intended to encourage creativity. The first was the time involved, as everyone had about a week to experience whatever they could in their chosen decade. (They were allowed to speed up time during the week, if needed.) The other was the freedom to time travel without the butterfly effect (i.e., unintended ripple effects) coming into the equation. So let’s have the chips fall wherever they may, and see what everyone came up with!


## Mid-1930s


dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images


I’ll go back to the mid-1930s, but I have to be wealthy and have the ability to own a Duesenberg, perhaps one like the[SSJ Special Speedster that won Best in Show](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/1935-duesenberg-ssj-special-speedster-wins-2026-pebble-beach-concours-delegance-best-of-show/) this year at the Pebble Beach Concours. I will have the wardrobe to match, and in my fantasies, I will drive the Duesy fast, and well, across Mulholland Drive, above Hollywood. — *Joe DeMatio*


## Just Make It Epic


Bettmann/Keystone/Getty Images


I think I’d go back to be on site for some sort of epic, historic race or event. First thing that comes to mind would be witnessing Stirling Moss’ Mille Miglia victory. Since we’re in a fantasy world, it would be fun to be able to witness every part of the race from wherever I wanted. Sub me in for Jenks as the navigator or just give me a helicopter to track the whole drive.


I would also love to see Senna drive in his prime. Put me right at the end of the ’80s and early ’90s where he’s winning everything. Dang, it would be awesome to just be at those F1 races and hear those cars all together at full throttle. As a bonus, I would also need to be on hand for him doing test drives of the NSX in his white socks and loafers. — *Ben Woodworth*


## The Last Open Roads?


ISC Archives/Getty Images


Sign me up for the 1950s. This was the last gasp of the open-road races, so I’d go on the Targa Florio, Mille Miglia, or the Carrera Panamericana. — *Larry Webster*


## Computer-Assisted Design, the Early Days


Buick


As much as I’d like to dive deep into pre-Depression 1920s automobile culture and listen to hot jazz music at the finest speakeasy in New York City, that’s really not true to me. I can’t waste this opportunity.


I constantly note how automobile design changed with the ability to create and implement/assemble vehicles with computer assistance. Whether it’s file sharing between factories and corporate offices, aerodynamic tweaks, engine tunes, or those awesome sales presentations on laser discs, well, I feel like I am already transported there. If only it could be real! — *Sajeev Mehta*


## May 1937, a Traffic-Free Los Angeles


I’d like to start in Los Angeles in May of 1937 and experience what this city was like when it was a small west-of-the-west town, before the post-war population boom. First stop would be a used car lot on Sunset where there would undoubtedly be an ex-studio exec Hispano-Suiza or Murphy-bodied Packard for sale for cheap. Then I would roam the two valleys enjoying the absence of traffic and run fast over Mulholland looking for Gary Cooper and Clark Gable racing their matching Duesenbergs. I would drop in at the Brown Derby, grab lunch at the Pig ‘n’ Whistle, and dine at Musso & Frank’s Grill to see what, if anything, is different about it today (besides the prices).


I would wander around the Hollywood Roosevelt and Biltmore looking for celebrities. Then I would drive across the USA to New York in time to see the Battle of the Bands between Benny Goodman and Chick Webb at the Savoy Ballroom in Harlem. I would park the car on the street, snap a bunch of pictures of it with my Leica Model E, and then just leave it there as the meter ran out on my time machine and I went ‘poof.’ When I got back to 2026, I would look up the current owner and offer him or her the pictures. Maybe for a small fee, depending on what the fare on the time machine cost. — *Aaron Robinson*


## Don’t Make Me Pick Just One!


ISC Archives/CQ-Roll Call Group/Getty Images


Huh. We pick an entire decade, but only get one specific week? Part 1, picking the decade, I can do. It starts in 1959, when the Daytona International Speedway opened, and closes in 1969 at the surreal debut of Talladega Speedway, where the drivers’ strike forced a lot of name-brand racers to watch from the wings.


But part 2, picking just a single week? Not sure I can. These 10 years of automotive development in general, and racing in particular, were pretty fascinating. Characters abounded. Deals were made. Hundred-aires became millionaires. But there must be opportunities in there for reflection, right? Here are some candidates.


Help me pick one week out of this: In 1960, I’d love to meet up with John Steinbeck and Charley, his poodle,[as they toured the country in Rocinante, their primitive GMC motorhome](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/a-writer-his-dog-and-a-chinook-follow-steinbecks-trail/) . I’d like to be up close for pivotal moments in Detroit as the auto industry invented the muscle car and its cousin, the pony car. It would be fun to look over the shoulder of John Delorean, plotting in his prime, and help Smokey Yunick beat NASCAR at its own game, and observe Dan Gurney invent the art of champagne spraying when he and A.J. Foyt won Le Mans in 1967 in a Ford GT. In the same year, Gurney drove his own homebuilt Eagle to victory in the F1 Belgian Grand Prix, beating Jackie Stewart and Jimmy Clark.


Of course, I would like to have been there when Clark and his rear-engine Lotus won the 1965 Indianapolis 500. I could counsel Cadillac on the design and presumed lifespan of tailfins, help Zora Arkus-Duntov with his little on-again, off-again Corvette project and Carroll Shelby with his Cobra. Maybe for several days of my week, I could stop by Woodstock and inhale a little musical culture. Yeah, that all sounds like important fun, and as long as we’re just dreaming, I think I’m gonna need the whole 10 years. — *Steven Cole Smith*


I was going to choose the 1910s or 1920s, because I’d love to experience what it was like when the automobile was transitioning from novelty to mainstream, cementing its place in our society, which it has changed forever. I’d love to see the weird and wonderful ways that Model Ts were adapted for various tasks (heck, even the later Model A was repurposed as[a mobile air compressor](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/when-america-reinvented-a-ford-to-get-stuff-done/) ), as horse-less power became readily available. But after reading SCS’s entry? I’ll have what *he’s* having, thanks. *— Grace Jarvis*


## Road Atlanta, October 1979


Porsche


I’d talk my way onto[Paul Newman’s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/paul-newman/) racing crew for the SCCA Runoffs at Road Atlanta from October 22–28, 1979. The Runoffs remain the pinnacle of amateur road racing in the States, but back then the stakes were higher and the fields deeper.


Maybe it’d be a bad idea to meet my actual hero at a hero track in a hero-level event, but I’m dying to know what it took to be a successful “amateur” at one of the sport’s high points. — *Eddy Eckart*
